# Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training

Ulyana Tkachenko^(\*) Affiliation: Handshake AI    Hui Wen Goh^(\*)
Affiliation: Handshake AI    Guram Gogia Affiliation: Handshake AI   
Jonas Mueller Affiliation: Handshake AI

###### Abstract

Rubrics enable reward assignment on tasks without verifiable answers,
but are expensive to manually produce from scratch. We present
_Rubricon_, a pipeline that generates discriminative rubrics without
requiring human preference labels, rubric annotation, or generator-model
training. Using any LLM, Rubricon samples multiple rubrics, selects the
most discriminative candidate, adds criteria to capture overlooked
requirements or response flaws, and prunes criteria that are misaligned
or shallow. Alongside LLM self-critique and test-time scaling, Rubricon
uses observed criterion pass rates on example model responses to guide
refinement. Across five professional, consumer, clinical, and
general-use LLM benchmarks, Rubricon produces rubrics whose scores of
frontier LLM responses exhibit 9% greater alignment with labor-intensive
expert-authored rubrics, compared to the best alternative synthetic
rubric generation method among RRD, QSRG, OpenRubrics, and agentic
generation via harnesses like Codex. On HealthBench, post-training a
Qwen3.5-9B model with Rubricon rubrics yields 4.5% better performance
than training with rubrics from the strongest alternative synthetic
rubric generator, RRD.

## 1 Introduction

Rubrics provide explicit, checkable criteria for systematically
evaluating open-domain LLM responses and assigning post-training rewards
([Gunjal et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11);
[Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib12)). Expert-authored rubrics are the gold
standard but are painstaking to produce (datasets with rubrics can
require hundreds of physicians or bankers ([Arora et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18); [Lau et al., 2026](#bib.bib3))). Asking an LLM to
generate a rubric yields criteria too shallow to separate strong
responses from weak ones, or even criteria that incorrectly favor
lower-quality responses ([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)). A further challenge is building rubrics that remain
discriminative as models improve, which requires criteria that will
appropriately penalize flaws in responses from stronger _future_ models
not yet available.

We propose _Rubricon_, a straightforward pipeline that automatically
generates higher-quality rubrics via three stages: Generate-and-Select,
Add, and Prune. It targets three properties a good rubric needs: (i) the
ability to discriminate between responses of different quality, (ii)
coverage so that substantively weak responses do not go unpenalized, and
(iii) headroom for quantifying flaws in responses from stronger future
models. The pipeline does not require any human data annotation or model
fine-tuning, and can utilize _any_ LLM to generate/refine the rubrics,
yielding better rubrics as LLMs advance. Rubricon also supports
iterative refinement as the Add and Prune stages can be repeatedly
applied to continuously reassess and improve a rubric’s criteria.

Rubricon illustrates a way to scale _test-time compute_ ([Snell et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)) for rubric generation that is empirically more
effective than alternate approaches like agentic rubric generation or
Recursive Rubric Decomposition ([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)). Relying
solely on LLM self-critique or ensembling yields limited test-time
scaling gains due to LLM brittleness and biases in the rubric generation
setting. Instead, Rubricon additionally grounds its refinement stages in
how candidate rubrics actually score example responses. Because existing
LLMs cannot properly self-judge their own generated rubrics, our
refinement stages encourage the models to rely on particular outside
signals and workflows which simplify the judgment calls a model must
make. Compared to existing rubric-generation techniques, the resulting
Rubricon-generated rubrics score responses more consistently with
expert-authored rubrics (Table
[1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.1 Alignment with Human Rubrics ‣ 6 Results for LLM Evaluation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"))
and improve post-training outcomes (Figure
[2](#S7.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Held-out policy evaluation. ‣ 7 Using Rubrics for Post-Training ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).

## 2 Related Work

Synthetic rubrics offer a structured alternative to holistic evaluation,
providing explicit, interpretable criteria for open-ended tasks and
post-training rewards ([Gunjal et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Huang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib11); [Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib12)). However, naively
generated synthetic rubrics can omit relevant dimensions or contain
generic, conflated, or misaligned criteria, reducing judgment accuracy
([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)). One omission from much of the existing
literature is evaluating how well a model’s synthetic rubrics score
responses from future stronger models. In practice, that is how
synthetic rubrics would advance the frontier of AI in non-verifiable
domains, especially if these rubrics are subsequently edited/validated
by experts and must provide lasting value that justifies this effort.

##### Rubric construction strategies.

AutoChecklist ([Zhou and Tan, 2026](#bib.bib1)) considers five paradigms
for rubric generation and validation: direct prompting, contrastive
generation, inductive extraction from feedback, decomposition of
predefined dimensions, and interactive construction using human and LLM
feedback. Response-grounded approaches to rubric-generation derive
discriminative criteria from observed quality differences between
candidate responses ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib14); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)). RubricRAG ([Dhole and Agichtein, 2026](#bib.bib15))
instead retrieves rubrics for similar queries and uses them as few-shot
examples to guide generation.

Our method simply generates an initial draft rubric via a single LLM
call, using a prompt that encodes general best practices ([Rao and
Callison-Burch, 2026](#bib.bib4)). This allows Rubricon to be flexibly
tailored for various settings where auxiliary inputs can be included in
this LLM call, such as when there are expert-written golden responses,
unstructured notes on what makes a response good/bad, critiques of
particular responses or expert-preferences between them, or few-shot
examples of expert-crafted rubrics. Rubricon’s refinement stages can be
applied to initial draft rubrics generated from any other approach.

##### Iterative and adaptive refinement.

Recursive Rubric Decomposition (RRD) ([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib7))
recursively decomposes broad criteria into finer-grained dimensions
while filtering misaligned and redundant criteria. Its whitened-uniform
(WU) variant further applies correlation-aware weighting of rubric
criteria to prevent overlapping criteria from dominating the aggregate
score. Other refinement approaches include: RubricHub ([Li et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)), which combines criteria from multiple models and
compares high-quality responses; Chasing the Tail ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)), which constructs discriminative rubrics from strong,
diverse responses to mitigate reward over-optimization; and SibylSense
([Xu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib16)), which adapts a frozen rubric-generator
through a memory bank of validated criteria, alternating verifier-guided
updates with adversarial generation of candidate responses.

##### Training rubric generators.

OpenRubrics ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)) uses contrastive prompting
to derive hard rules and implicit principles from prompts and
preference-ordered responses, then fine-tunes a rubric generator and
judge on examples filtered for preference consistency. [Lv et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib22) train a query-specific rubric generator (QSRG)
through reinforcement learning, rewarding human-preference consistency,
format validity, and LLM-assessed rubric quality. [Sheng et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib17) jointly train one model for reasoning and rubric
generation, using evolving criteria for chain-of-thought supervision.

## 3 Task Formulation

We consider open-ended tasks, each specified by a prompt $`T`$ for which
a model should generate a response. A rubric for $`T`$ is a set of
weighted binary criteria $`\mathcal{R}=\{(c_{k},w_{k})\}_{k=1}^{m}`$
used to grade any possible response, where each criterion $`c_{k}`$ is a
binary (pass/fail) natural-language requirement and $`w_{k}`$ encodes
its relative importance. A _verifier_ model $`v(c_{k},y)\in\{0,1\}`$
judges whether response $`y`$ satisfies each criterion $`c_{k}`$. The
response $`y`$ receives an overall normalized score:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
s_{\mathcal{R}}(y)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{m}w_{k}\,v(c_{k},y)}{\sum_{k=1}^{m}\max(w_{k},0)}
``` |  | (1) |

We use this score to rank responses from different models or as rewards
in post-training. While Rubricon’s rubrics employ positive weights for
simplicity, some rubrics contain negative-weight criteria (including
baseline methods we compare against in our experiments).

A strong rubric satisfies three *desiderata*:

1.  1.
    Discrimination. The rubric should assign higher scores to
    higher-quality responses, clearly separating better from worse.
2.  2.
    Coverage. The rubric should capture relevant requirements and
    failure modes that models actually exhibit, so that flawed responses
    do not receive high scores.
3.  3.
    Headroom. The rubric should remain sensitive to meaningful quality
    differences among responses from future models, even as their
    capabilities improve.

Due to verifier noise and computation costs as well as
human-editing/review costs, more criteria are not always desirable in a
rubric. A rubric should instead have the fewest criteria that achieve
the aforementioned desiderata, and should not include basic criteria
that any existing model would pass or subjective/complex criteria that a
simple verifier model cannot reliably grade.

![Refer to caption](2610.38220v1/artifacts/figs/rubricon_pipeline.png)

Figure 1: The Rubricon pipeline. Given a task prompt, example
strong-model responses, and optional reference material,
Generate-and-Select drafts $`K=5`$ candidate rubrics and selects the
rubric with the largest average strong–weak edge across criteria. Add
sequentially expands the selected rubric through gap fill, prompt
coverage, negative probing, and completeness probing, with each step
operating on the rubric from the prior step. The probe steps generate
responses intended to satisfy the current rubric, then convert
independently identified defects or omissions into new criteria. Prune
removes misaligned criteria and those that are satisfiable by evasive or
weak responses. The resulting rubric can undergo further Add then Prune
refinement rounds.

## 4 Rubricon

Rubricon constructs and refines rubrics through a modular pipeline that
can utilize any off-the-shelf LLM as the *generator model*. Unlike
rubric generators that require model training, the performance of our
approach can be instantly improved whenever better LLMs are released.
Rubricon can also leverage expert reference responses or expert
reasoning as additional context whenever available for a task. It
measures criterion pass rates on sample responses and uses LLM-based
checks to identify missing requirements and poorly formulated criteria.
Its main discriminative signal is the *strong–weak edge*, the gap in
criterion pass rates between stronger- and weaker-model responses,
adapted from the misalignment filter proposed by [Shen et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib7). The pipeline uses these signals to select an initial
rubric, add missing criteria, and remove misaligned criteria or criteria
that are satisfiable by evasive or weak responses.

### 4.1 Aspects of Effective Rubric Criteria

Beyond the rubric-level desiderata in Section
[3](#S3 "3 Task Formulation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"),
a good rubric requires well-formed individual criteria. We enumerate a
universal set of Criteria Principles, a task-agnostic style guide for
writing criteria, which we embed into our criterion generation steps.
Each criterion should be clear and unambiguous, with an explicit pass
condition; self-contained, requiring no external references to assess
the response; atomic, testing only one requirement; and free of
cross-references, requiring no other criterion or verdict to interpret.
These principles govern individual criteria, while the Rubricon pipeline
in Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Rubricon Pipeline ‣ 4 Rubricon ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
operates on the criterion set. Appendix
[F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Criteria Principles ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
presents the Criteria Principles guide.

In our rubrics, each criterion contains: criterion text, a
natural-language requirement that is straightforward to objectively
judge as pass or fail; an importance label, which determines its weight
in the aggregate score (Eq.
[1](#S3.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 3 Task Formulation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"));
and a category, such as Factual Accuracy, Reasoning, or Safety.
Categories describe the dimension of the response being assessed but do
not affect its score according to the rubric. Our rubric generator
assigns each criterion an importance label: Critical, Major, or Minor,
for which we assign relative importance weights of 5, 3, and 1,
respectively ([Gunjal et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Lau et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3); [Lommel et al., 2024](#bib.bib5); [Rao and
Callison-Burch, 2026](#bib.bib4)).

### 4.2 The Rubricon Pipeline

Rubricon generates and refines rubrics through three stages:
Generate-and-Select, Add, and Prune (Figure
[1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Task Formulation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
Criteria generated throughout the pipeline follow the Criteria
Principles in Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Aspects of Effective Rubric Criteria ‣ 4 Rubricon ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").
The three pipeline stages address the rubric-level desiderata in Section
[3](#S3 "3 Task Formulation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"):
Generate-and-Select targets discrimination, Add expands coverage and
helps distinguish among stronger responses, and Prune removes criteria
that reward wrong qualities or lead to noisy scores.

Before running Rubricon to produce a rubric for a prompt, one first
generates a set of example responses to the prompt, some from a known
*stronger* model (e.g. GPT-6) and some from a known *weaker* model (e.g.
GPT-4). While one cannot guarantee that the weaker model’s response is
not better than the stronger model’s, appropriately choosing these LLMs
makes this unlikely.

##### Generate-and-Select.

We generate $`K=5`$ candidate rubrics through independent LLM calls for
which the input is the task prompt, example responses (from only the
strong-model), and any task-provided reference context from experts
(Appendix
[F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Rubric Generation ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
Generating multiple rubric candidates broadens coverage and reduces
reliance on any single draft, while retaining alternative criteria for
the subsequent Add stage. To choose the best initial draft rubric among
these candidates, we assess how well their criteria distinguish
stronger- from weaker-model responses.

A criterion satisfied by every example response provides no
discrimination among those responses, whereas one that weaker-model
responses pass more often than stronger-model responses suggests
misalignment. Following [Shen et al. (2026)](#bib.bib7), we quantify
this using the *strong–weak edge*: the difference in a criterion’s pass
rates between stronger- and weaker-model responses, for which we first
run the verifier to score these example responses against the draft
rubric criteria.

Let $`Y_{s}`$ and $`Y_{w}`$ denote the stronger- and weaker-model
response sets, respectively, and let $`\bar{v}(c,y)`$ denote the
verifier pass rate over $`n`$ judgments for criterion $`c`$ against
response $`y`$. We estimate the strong–weak edge as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
e(c)=\frac{1}{|Y_{s}|}\sum_{y\in Y_{s}}\bar{v}(c,y)-\frac{1}{|Y_{w}|}\sum_{y\in Y_{w}}\bar{v}(c,y)
``` |  | (2) |

A positive edge indicates that stronger-model responses satisfy the
criterion more often, suggesting it discriminates in the right
direction.

We rely on these edge estimates in both rubric candidate selection and
criterion filtering stages. In the selection stage, Rubricon retains the
candidate rubric with the highest average strong–weak edge, where this
average is computed over all criteria in the rubric. The criteria in the
unselected rubrics are considered a candidate pool for the subsequent
Add stage.

##### Add missing coverage.

Even the selected candidate rubric remains unlikely to satisfy all
desiderata in Section
[3](#S3 "3 Task Formulation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").
To expand coverage and target headroom, Rubricon refines this draft
rubric through four complementary addition stages, applied sequentially
so that each operates on the rubric augmented by the preceding stages:

1.  1.
    Gap fill retrieves non-redundant criteria from the unselected
    candidate rubrics to cover expectations missing from the current
    rubric (Appendix
    [F.2.1](#A6.SS2.SSS1 "F.2.1 Gap Fill ‣ F.2 Add Stage ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
    It first filters the candidate criteria pool such that a criterion
    is ignored if every example response passes it in every verifier
    run, or if every strong-model response fails it and every weak-model
    response passes it in every verifier run.
2.  2.
    Prompt coverage checks whether the rubric captures explicit task
    requirements. The task’s prompt is decomposed into atomic
    requirements, each marked as covered, partially covered, or
    uncovered by the current rubric. Uncovered or partially covered
    requirements are converted into new criteria (Appendix
    [F.2.2](#A6.SS2.SSS2 "F.2.2 Prompt Coverage ‣ F.2 Add Stage ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
3.  3.
    Negative probing generates adversarially-weak responses (from the
    same LLM) that are known to be bad but that the current rubric may
    overlook. A separate LLM reviewer, seeing only the task and one such
    response, flags concrete defects. A subsequent LLM call converts
    relevant defects not already covered by the rubric into new criteria
    (Appendix
    [F.2.3](#A6.SS2.SSS3 "F.2.3 Negative Probing ‣ F.2 Add Stage ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
4.  4.
    Completeness probing searches for omissions in an intended
    high-quality response. A model is prompted to generate a response
    that satisfies every criterion in the current rubric. A separate LLM
    reviewer, seeing only the task prompt and response, flags missing or
    incomplete information that a high-quality answer would still need.
    A final LLM call converts relevant omissions not already covered by
    the rubric into new criteria (Appendix
    [F.2.4](#A6.SS2.SSS4 "F.2.4 Completeness Probing ‣ F.2 Add Stage ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).

These four stages expand rubric coverage. Newly generated criteria
follow the Criteria Principles and receive importance labels as
described in Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Aspects of Effective Rubric Criteria ‣ 4 Rubricon ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").
The model is instructed to add only task-relevant criteria that are not
already covered in the current rubric and are not overly specific to a
particular solution approach. We subsequently use the verifier to score
the sample responses against each newly added criterion, allowing
misaligned criteria to be identified and removed during pruning.

##### Prune misleading criteria.

Generation and expansion can introduce noisy criteria that degrade
response scoring. To support discrimination after expansion, we remove a
criterion if its estimated strong–weak edge (Eq.
[2](#S4.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ Generate-and-Select. ‣ 4.2 The Rubricon Pipeline ‣ 4 Rubricon ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"))
is below a threshold ($`-0.10`$), or if an LLM assessor flags it as
satisfiable by an evasive or weak response (Appendix
[F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 Prune: Shallow-Criterion Assessor ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).

The remaining criteria form the refined rubric. Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Rubricon Refinement Examples ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
provides examples showing how the Add and Prune stages update a specific
rubric’s criteria.

##### Iterative refinement.

The Add and Prune stages can be repeatedly iterated. We refer to one
application of Add followed by Prune as a refinement round, with each
subsequent round starting from the preceding round’s refined rubric. Gap
fill continues to draw from the original unselected drafts, while
coverage checks and probes are rerun against the updated rubric. The
same strong- and weak-model responses are reused to score and prune
criteria across rounds. After a second refinement round, we consistently
observe higher alignment with expert-authored rubrics (Section
[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Iterative Refinement Across Multiple Rounds ‣ 6 Results for LLM Evaluation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).

## 5 Experimental Setup

### 5.1 Assessing Rubric Quality

We assess the quality of each generated rubric by how well the resulting
rubric scores align with expert human judgments of the same responses.

##### Alignment with expert-authored rubrics.

Human-written criteria describe what experts expect from a good response
and can rank responses by how well they meet those expectations.
Agreement with these rankings tests whether generated rubrics capture
similar quality distinctions, even if the rubrics assign different
numerical scores. To quantify this alignment, we use the verifier to
score a set of *assessment responses* from many models against both
auto-generated and expert-authored rubrics, then rank the responses
according to each rubric, and finally report Spearman’s rank correlation
($`\rho`$) between these two rankings. The overall alignment for a
dataset is the average $`\rho`$ across all of its tasks.

##### Alignment with human preferences.

Human pairwise preferences between two responses provide an alternative
measure of quality, albeit often coarser/noisier than rubric-based
scoring ([Rezaei et al., 2026](#bib.bib8); [Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib9)). Alignment with these preferences indicates how well
rubric scores reflect human assessments of relative response quality. We
report selective preference accuracy: after scoring all responses
against the generated rubric, we retain response-pairs whose normalized
rubric scores differ by more than a fixed margin ($`\delta=0.10`$) and
measure how often the higher-scoring response matches the human
preference. We use this margin to avoid treating small score differences
that may arise from verifier variability as meaningful preferences.

### 5.2 Verifier Scoring

Our verifier $`v(c,y)\in\{0,1\}`$ is an LLM that judges whether a
response $`y`$ satisfies a criterion $`c`$. As in [Wang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib19), the verifier receives only the response and a
single criterion, without the original task prompt, under the assumption
that criteria are self-contained and can be judged independently. To
account for variability in its judgments, we evaluate each
response-criterion pair $`n`$ times using the prompt in Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Verifier Prompt ‣ Appendix B Details about the Verifier Model ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"),
denoting the verdict from the $`j`$-th evaluation by $`v_{j}(c,y)`$.
Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Details about the Verifier Model ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
shows that our verifier exhibits high agreement with expert judgments
when grading the same responses against the same rubrics.

##### Verifier scoring within the Rubricon pipeline.

For rubric selection and pruning, we sample five responses from a
stronger model and three from a weaker model per task. Each
response-criterion pair receives $`n=3`$ verifier evaluations. We
average all verifier judgments of each model’s example responses to
obtain its pass rate for a criterion, then subtract the weaker model’s
pass rate from the stronger model’s to estimate the strong–weak edge
defined in Eq.
[2](#S4.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ Generate-and-Select. ‣ 4.2 The Rubricon Pipeline ‣ 4 Rubricon ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").

##### Verifier scoring for rubric-quality assessment.

For assessing rubric quality, we apply the verifier to completed rubrics
and fixed responses separate from those used during rubric construction.
The verifier produces $`n=3`$ judgments for each response-criterion
pair. We aggregate the $`j`$-th judgment across all criteria to obtain a
response score for scoring run $`j`$, using Eq.
[1](#S3.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 3 Task Formulation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").

For alignment with expert-authored rubrics, we use both
automatically-generated and human-written rubrics to score the same set
of assessment responses from various LLMs. Within each scoring run, we
compute $`\rho`$ between the two sets of response scores, yielding $`n`$
correlation estimates per task. We report the mean correlation across
all tasks and scoring runs within each benchmark. For selective
preference accuracy, we apply the margin to each of the $`n`$ score
comparisons for a task, then pool the retained comparisons across all
tasks to compute accuracy.

### 5.3 Datasets

We evaluate the generated rubrics on five benchmarks spanning
professional, consumer, clinical, and general-purpose tasks (Table
[3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ A.3 Data Preprocessing ‣ Appendix A Benchmark Dataset Details ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
We use expert-authored rubrics from ProfBench ([Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib19)), PRBench ([Akyürek et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)), ACE
([Benchek et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)), and HealthBench ([Arora et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18)) to measure alignment between rankings of different
LLM responses produced by generated v.s. expert-authored rubrics. We use
human preference labels from RubricBench ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)) to measure human preference agreement. Dataset
descriptions, preprocessing, reference material, and final task counts
are detailed in Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Benchmark Dataset Details ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").

### 5.4 Baselines

We compare Rubricon against two families of baselines described in
Section
[2](#S2 "2 Related Work ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"):
prompt-based methods, including an Agentic baseline (Appendix
[G](#A7 "Appendix G Agent Rubric Generation Baseline ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"))
and RRD_(WU) ([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)), and post-trained rubric
generators, including the Query-Specific Rubric Generator (QSRG) ([Lv et
al., 2026](#bib.bib22)) and OpenRubrics ([Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)). Rubricon belongs to the prompt-based family. Each
method produces one rubric per task, and across all five benchmarks,
responses are graded against these rubrics using the same verifier and
$`n=3`$ replicate scoring runs (Section
[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Verifier Scoring ‣ 5 Experimental Setup ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).

The *Agentic* baseline runs in a Codex SDK ([OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib24))
harness with full local tool access and web access disabled, freely
choosing its rubric-construction procedure. It tests whether an
unconstrained agent can match Rubricon’s structured pipeline. Appendix
[G](#A7 "Appendix G Agent Rubric Generation Baseline ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
provides details. Both the Agentic and RRD baselines receive the same
task prompt, example model responses, and available reference material
as Rubricon (Section
[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Datasets ‣ 5 Experimental Setup ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).

The post-trained rubric generators, OpenRubrics and QSRG, are run as
published and receive the task prompt alone. We also examine the effect
of input context through QSRG+Context, which uses the same trained
generator as query-only QSRG, but augments the task query with example
model responses and any dataset-provided reference material (Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Benchmark Dataset Details ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
The post-trained rubric generators use their respective models: QSRG and
QSRG+Context use a Qwen3-30B-A3B-based generator, while OpenRubrics uses
Rubric-RM-8B, based on Qwen3-8B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)).

### 5.5 Models Employed

For experiments measuring alignment with human rubrics and human
preferences, all prompt-based rubric generation methods, including
Rubricon, are powered by the same generator model: GPT-5.1.

For rubric generation methods that leverage example LLM responses during
rubric construction, we use responses from GPT-5.1 and
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ([Grattafiori et al., 2024](#bib.bib27)) as the
*strong* and *weak* models, respectively. We use GPT-5 mini as the
verifier model for criterion grading throughout, because this model was
observed to provide a favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff, with strong
agreement with human expert judgments on the same responses and rubrics
(Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Agreement with Expert Human Graders ‣ Appendix B Details about the Verifier Model ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).

For our experiments measuring alignment with human rubrics, we use
generated rubrics to score a separate set of responses from the
following models: GPT-5.2 Instant, GPT-5.2 Thinking, Claude Sonnet 4.6,
Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3
Flash, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. We generate one response from each model per
task, yielding eight responses to score with each rubric (not used
during rubric construction). Appendix
[C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Model Inference Settings ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
reports inference settings.

Some of these responses come from newer/stronger models than those used
for rubric generation and verification. This reflects the fact that good
rubrics must remain useful for evaluating responses from future models,
which remains underexplored in prior work. [Shen et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib7), [Xu et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib16), and [Zhang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib2) evaluate their generated rubrics mainly on responses
from models weaker than or comparable to the rubric generator, although
some of them leverage responses from stronger models during rubric
construction.

## 6 Results for LLM Evaluation

Unless otherwise specified, Rubricon results are for the rubric obtained
after two refinement rounds.

### 6.1 Alignment with Human Rubrics

Rubricon achieves the highest $`\rho`$ on all four benchmarks in Table
[1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.1 Alignment with Human Rubrics ‣ 6 Results for LLM Evaluation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").
It attains a macro-average $`\rho`$ of $`0.428`$ across these datasets,
representing a $`9.0\%`$ relative improvement over RRD_(WU), the
strongest alternative approach. On ACE, Rubricon exceeds the next-best
method by $`0.052`$, its largest margin across the four benchmarks.
Additional context improves QSRG on three benchmarks, but overall both
post-trained rubric generators produce substantially less expert-aligned
rubrics than Rubricon.

| QSRG | $`0.361\pm 0.082`$ | $`0.225\pm 0.043`$ | $`0.226\pm 0.013`$ | $`0.172\pm 0.008`$ | $`52.9\pm 1.6`$ |

| RRD_(WU) | $`0.394\pm 0.076`$ | $`0.316\pm 0.040`$ | $`0.497\pm 0.011`$ | $`0.365\pm 0.009`$ | $`58.7\pm 1.7`$ |
| Rubricon | $`\mathbf{0.424\pm 0.083}`$ | $`\mathbf{0.385\pm 0.035}`$ | $`\mathbf{0.516\pm 0.011}`$ | $`\mathbf{0.388\pm 0.009}`$ | $`\mathbf{59.8\pm 1.9}`$ |

Table 1: Alignment with human rubrics and human preferences. Rubricon
achieves the highest observed scores across all five benchmarks. Across
datasets, it improves macro-average $`\rho`$ by 9.0% relative to the
strongest baseline, RRD_(WU) ($`0.428`$ vs. $`0.393`$), and selective
preference accuracy by 0.5 percentage points over the strongest
preference baseline, Agentic ($`59.8\%`$ vs. $`59.3\%`$). The first four
benchmarks report $`\rho`$ between scores under generated and
expert-authored rubrics. RubricBench reports selective preference
accuracy (%), evaluated on response pairs whose normalized rubric scores
differ by more than $`0.10`$ (retained counts in Table
[7](#A3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ C.1 Rubric Sizes and Retained Human Preference Comparisons ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
The $`\pm`$ values indicate standard errors estimated by bootstrapping
tasks ($`B=500`$ resamples).

### 6.2 Alignment with Human Preference

Rubricon achieves the highest observed selective preference accuracy,
exceeding the next-best method, the Agentic baseline, by $`0.5`$
percentage points (rightmost column in Table
[1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.1 Alignment with Human Rubrics ‣ 6 Results for LLM Evaluation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
Note that the alignment with human preferences is fairly low for all
methods, because [Zhou et al. (2026)](#bib.bib23) purposefully populated
RubricBench with challenging examples.

### 6.3 Iterative Refinement Across Multiple Rounds

Rubricon is an iterative pipeline: the Add and Prune stages can be
reapplied to refine the rubric produced by the preceding round. Table
[8](#A3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ C.2 Detailed Performance Across Refinement Steps ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
shows that the first refinement round yields an $`11.9\%`$ relative
improvement in macro-average $`\rho`$ over the selected initial rubric.
The second round yields a further $`5.1\%`$ relative improvement over
the first round. Compared with RRD_(WU), the relative improvements after
one and two rounds are $`3.7\%`$ and $`9.0\%`$, respectively.

### 6.4 Performance Across Refinement Steps

We examine the contribution of each pipeline stage by assessing the
quality of intermediate rubrics produced during the first refinement
round. Table
[2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6.4 Performance Across Refinement Steps ‣ 6 Results for LLM Evaluation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
summarizes results across the four benchmarks with expert-authored
rubrics. Detailed per-benchmark results appear in Table
[9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.2 Detailed Performance Across Refinement Steps ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").
The results show that each stage of the Rubricon pipeline is valuable:
every stage improves alignment on at least one benchmark, and most
stages also improve the macro-average $`\rho`$ across the four
benchmarks. These results suggest that different stages are useful for
different types of tasks, which could differ substantially in their
expert-authored rubrics and what constitutes a good response.

Some steps in the Add stage slightly reduce macro-average $`\rho`$ while
improving this alignment with expert-rubrics on individual benchmarks.
Expanding rubric coverage can introduce noisy or misleading criteria
alongside useful ones. Subsequent pruning is designed to remove these
problematic criteria and proves empirically effective overall. The
improvement in alignment after pruning suggests that coverage expansion
and filtering play complementary roles, even when gains are not observed
immediately after the Add step.

|----------------------|-----------------------|--------------------|
| Stage                |  Macro-avg. $`\rho`$  |  Avg. Rubric Size  |
| Generation           | 0.359                 | 20.6               |
| Selected Rubric      | 0.364                 | 20.6               |
| Gap Fill             | 0.362                 | 23.9               |
| Prompt Coverage      | 0.362                 | 24.6               |
| Negative Probing     | 0.388                 | 28.3               |
| Completeness Probing | 0.395                 | 31.0               |
| Prune                | 0.408                 | 26.7               |

are averaged over $`K=5`$ independently generated rubrics.

## 7 Using Rubrics for Post-Training

Beyond model evaluation, rubrics are also used to compute rewards for
post-training LLMs via reinforcement learning. Here we assess how
effective Rubricon rubrics are for RL post-training of the Qwen3.5-9B
model ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib29)). Our experiment trains the same
model using the same recipe against rubrics from different generators,
and then measures the quality of each resulting model based on how it
scores against expert-authored rubrics for held-out tasks.

##### Data.

We post-train models on the HealthBench dataset, randomly splitting its
1,704 prompts into 1,204 training prompts and 500 held-out evaluation
prompts.

##### Training conditions.

We compare two training-time reward sources: RRD_(WU), our strongest
baseline for alignment with expert-authored rubrics, and Rubricon
rubrics obtained after two refinement rounds. We fine-tune the released
Qwen3.5-9B model checkpoint with GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib25))
for eight epochs. Training configurations are detailed in Appendix
[C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Post-training details ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"),
Table
[11](#A3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ C.5 Post-training details ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").
Apart from the training-time rubrics, the model, training recipe, data
split, and evaluation procedure are held fixed.

##### Held-out policy evaluation.

At each evaluated model checkpoint, we sample three independent
responses per held-out prompt and score them against physician-authored
HealthBench criteria (using the same verifier). We report avg@3, the
average of the (expert-authored) rubric scores of these three
independently sampled responses, subsequently averaged across all
held-out evaluation prompts. We also report paired 95% bootstrap
confidence intervals for the difference in mean scores between models
trained using different rubrics.

![Refer to
caption](2610.38220v1/artifacts/figs/healthbench_posttraining.png)

Figure 2: Rubricon rewards translate into stronger held-out
post-training performance. Qwen3.5-9B trained with Rubricon rubric
rewards outperforms the same model trained with RRD_(WU) rewards at
every evaluated post-training checkpoint, reaching a 4.5% higher score
at the last evaluated checkpoint. Scores are averaged over three
independently sampled responses per prompt, then across 500 held-out
HealthBench prompts. The Rubricon-trained model achieves a 20.5% higher
held-out score than the starting model checkpoint.

##### Results.

Under the fixed recipe, training with Rubricon rubrics yields higher
held-out HealthBench scores than training with RRD_(WU) rubrics at every
evaluated checkpoint (Figure
[2](#S7.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Held-out policy evaluation. ‣ 7 Using Rubrics for Post-Training ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
The final-checkpoint improvement is $`0.0315`$ (paired 95% bootstrap CI:
$`[+0.0207,+0.0427]`$). Here we use Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite as the
verifier model for both rollout scoring during training and held-out
evaluation graded against expert-authored rubrics. The advantage
persists when the same final-checkpoint responses are re-scored by GPT-5
mini or Claude Sonnet 5 as verifiers instead (Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Post-training Results Across Verifiers ‣ Appendix B Details about the Verifier Model ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
These results support Rubricon’s efficacy for providing reward signals
in post-training.

## 8 Discussion

Our results show that rubric quality can be automatically improved
beyond basic LLM or agentic generation, without requiring additional
data collection/annotation or model fine-tuning. By systematically
selecting discriminative drafts, filling gaps in coverage, and removing
misleading criteria, Rubricon produces more effective rubrics for LLM
evaluation and training. The key is a methodical test-time scaling
strategy that does not purely rely on LLM self-critique and ensembling,
but additionally grounds refinement stages in how draft rubrics actually
score example responses.

## Limitations

Our experiments are limited to single-turn LLM responses in certain
domains and to the English language. It remains unclear whether the
rubrics generated in these experiments will continue to distinguish
response quality as models continue to improve beyond the most advanced
LLMs considered in our experiments. As models are increasingly trained
as agentic and multi-agent systems, an agentic or multi-agent approach
to rubric generation may one day surpass Rubricon.

Rubricon relies heavily on model-derived signals and the resulting
automatically generated rubrics are far from perfect. Because it is
compatible with any LLM, Rubricon rubrics will improve as models
improve, but the flaws in model responses will also get subtler. In
these non-verifiable domains where quality judgments are driven by
expert taste, one cannot rely on theoretical guarantees because what
constitutes a good rubric can greatly vary from one dataset to another.

Thus we recommend always having human experts review and improve the
rubrics automatically generated by methods like Rubricon, which still
yields enormous time-savings compared to manually crafting rubrics from
scratch. A beneficial property of our method is that its modular stages
are easy to adjust based on expert feedback, and a prompt-based approach
like ours can easily incorporate expert suggestions/conventions as well
(in contrast to a trained rubric generator). Rubricon’s refinement
stages can be seamlessly iterated with manual expert updates to rubrics,
or even applied to human-crafted initial rubrics. Optimal human-AI
collaboration to construct LLM evaluations effectively and affordably
remains an important topic for future research.

Appendix

## Appendix A Benchmark Dataset Details

### A.1 Benchmarks for Assessing Rubric Quality

##### Benchmarks with human rubrics.

To ensure they are high-quality, we first reviewed many expert-authored
rubrics in every dataset used in our experiments on alignment against
expert rubrics. Many other datasets were omitted from consideration
during these reviews.

We use the Finance, Consulting, and Physics domains of ProfBench ([Wang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)) and the Finance and Law tasks of PRBench
([Akyürek et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)). Both benchmarks contain tasks
requiring professional knowledge and reasoning. We also use the open
development split of the AI Consumer Index (ACE) ([Benchek et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21)), which covers everyday consumer tasks in Shopping,
DIY, Gaming, and Food, and HealthBench ([Arora et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18)), which contains health conversations with
physician-authored, importance-weighted rubrics. On these four
benchmarks, we score the same responses using generated and
expert-authored rubrics and report rank correlations as defined in
Section
[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Assessing Rubric Quality ‣ 5 Experimental Setup ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").
HealthBench is also used for post-training experiments because of its
size and prior work using generated rubrics as reinforcement-learning
rewards ([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)).

##### Benchmark with human preferences.

We use the released RubricBench preference set ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)), comprising 1,147 pairwise preference examples drawn
from datasets like HelpSteer3, PPE, and RewardBench2. Each example
contains a task, two LLM responses, and a binary human preference label.
We score each response independently using the generated rubric and
report selective preference accuracy defined in Section
[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Assessing Rubric Quality ‣ 5 Experimental Setup ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training").

### A.2 Reference Material for Rubric Construction

Rubricon, Agentic, RRD_(WU), and QSRG+Context are provided with task
prompts, example model responses, and any auxiliary per-task reference
material in each dataset (see Appendix
[F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Rubric Generation ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
This reference material includes expert-authored step-by-step reasoning
for PRBench and expert-authored example responses for HealthBench. We
treat the human-written responses in HealthBench as example responses
rather than golden reference completions, after finding that they do not
score highly under its own expert-authored rubrics. No additional
reference material is used for ProfBench, ACE, or RubricBench. QSRG and
OpenRubrics receive the task prompt alone. The expert-authored rubrics
used for alignment-evaluation are never provided to the
rubric-generators.

### A.3 Data Preprocessing

We filter our datasets to the subset of examples for which we are more
confident in the quality of expert-authored rubrics. We require at least
10 expert-authored criteria for ProfBench, PRBench, and HealthBench to
support graded, discriminative scoring and reduce ties. We do not apply
the 10-criterion minimum to ACE, whose human-authored rubrics contain 7
criteria on average. We restrict PRBench and HealthBench to single-turn
tasks and require expert-written responses as reference material for
HealthBench. We exclude ProfBench’s Chemistry domain after identifying
issues in the expert-authored rubrics, such as vague or hedged criteria
and inconsistent numerical-precision requirements. Table
[3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ A.3 Data Preprocessing ‣ Appendix A Benchmark Dataset Details ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
reports final task counts and the reference material used for each
dataset.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Benchmark | Domain(s) | Human annotations | Tasks | Ref. material |
| ProfBench | Finance, Consulting, Physics | Human rubrics | 28 | — |
| PRBench | Finance, Law | Human rubrics | 656 | expert step-by-step reasoning |
| ACE | Shopping, DIY, Gaming, Food | Human rubrics | 80 | — |
| HealthBench | Health | Human rubrics | 1,704 | example response |
| RubricBench | Chat, IF, STEM, Code, Safety | Human preferences | 1,147 | — |

Table 3: Evaluation benchmarks. Human annotations specifies how
generated rubrics are assessed: alignment with scores from
human-authored rubrics or human preferences between responses. Tasks
gives the number of tasks evaluated after preprocessing. Ref. material
lists the inputs provided for each task in the rubric generation prompt
(see Appendix
[F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Rubric Generation ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).

## Appendix B Details about the Verifier Model

### B.1 Agreement with Expert Human Graders

|                   |                    |           |            |           |
|-------------------|--------------------|-----------|------------|-----------|
|                   | Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ |           | F1         |           |
| Verifier Model    | Our Prompt         | ProfBench | Our Prompt | ProfBench |
| GPT-5 mini        | 0.581              | 0.549     | 0.802      | 0.786     |
| GPT-5.2           | 0.560              | 0.556     | 0.777      | 0.777     |
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | 0.556              | 0.533     | 0.785      | 0.760     |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro    | 0.580              | 0.582     | 0.791      | 0.794     |

Table 4: Using our verifier prompt, GPT-5 mini achieves the highest
observed Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ and F1 among the tested verifiers. We report
criterion-level agreement (Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ and F1) with expert
annotations on ProfBench using our judge prompt and the original
ProfBench judge prompt. On a 367-criterion subset that we independently
re-annotated, (non-expert) human agreement with the ProfBench expert
annotations is $`\kappa=0.281`$ (64.0% raw agreement). The GPT-5 mini
verifier reaches $`\kappa=0.455`$ (72.5% raw agreement) against the
expert labels on the same subset.

Rubric-based evaluation depends on the verifier’s ability to correctly
judge whether responses satisfy each criterion. To assess the quality of
the verifier used in our experiments, we compare LLM verifier judgments
with expert human annotations on over 3,400 response-criterion pairs
from ProfBench ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). For each pair, the
verifier is assessing the same response against the same expert-authored
criterion, with the purpose of measuring the criterion-level grading
accuracy, separate from the quality of generated rubrics.

We evaluate four verifier models with two prompts: our verifier prompt
(Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Verifier Prompt ‣ Appendix B Details about the Verifier Model ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")),
which we use for all our experiments, and the verifier prompt used by
ProfBench ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). Our prompt generally yields
higher agreement and F1 scores than the ProfBench prompt (Table
[4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.1 Agreement with Expert Human Graders ‣ Appendix B Details about the Verifier Model ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
GPT-5 mini achieves the best performance while remaining cost-effective
and highly stable. Across 8 repeated runs, GPT-5 mini’s judgments agree
on 97.2% of criteria (mean pairwise $`\kappa=0.943`$).

### B.2 Post-training Results Across Verifiers

To further validate the post-training results with alternative
verifiers, we re-scored the final-checkpoint responses with GPT-5 mini
and Claude Sonnet 5 on the same physician-authored HealthBench rubrics.
The results in Table
[5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.2 Post-training Results Across Verifiers ‣ Appendix B Details about the Verifier Model ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
confirm that Rubricon’s advantage over RRD_(WU) holds across all three
verifier models.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Verifier Model | RRD_(WU) | Rubricon | $`\Delta\pm\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{paired}}`$ |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite | 0.7077 | 0.7392 | $`0.0315\pm 0.0057`$ |
| GPT-5 mini | 0.6482 | 0.6753 | $`0.0271\pm 0.0052`$ |
| Claude Sonnet 5 | 0.5357 | 0.5710 | $`0.0353\pm 0.0059`$ |

Table 5: Verifier sensitivity on held-out HealthBench evaluation
dataset. Each verifier scores the same saved responses from the two
policies after eight training epochs against physician-authored rubrics.
$`\Delta`$ denotes Rubricon minus RRD_(WU). Standard errors are computed
across paired prompt-level differences.

### C.3 Rubric Size and Category Composition

![Refer to caption](2610.38220v1/artifacts/figs/category_share.png)

Figure 3: Rubric category composition across different benchmarks and
pipeline stages during Rubricon’s first refinement round. Each benchmark
has a different category distribution more representative of its domain,
but all show a $`33`$–$`45\%`$ relative increase in the share of
Reasoning criteria during refinement.

|             |                     |      |       |         |       |
|-------------|---------------------|------|-------|---------|-------|
|             | Round 1             |      |       | Round 2 |       |
| Dataset     | Generate-and-Select | Add  | Prune | Add     | Prune |
| ProfBench   | 23.6                | 37.3 | 32.8  | 46.1    | 41.9  |
| PRBench     | 21.3                | 34.1 | 31.4  | 40.5    | 38.8  |
| ACE         | 19.4                | 27.5 | 22.0  | 29.5    | 25.0  |
| HealthBench | 17.9                | 25.0 | 20.5  | 26.2    | 23.4  |
| RubricBench | 15.8                | 21.0 | 17.1  | 21.5    | 18.8  |

Table 10: Mean rubric size (criteria per task) at each pipeline stage,
averaged over all tasks in each evaluation dataset. In Round 1, Add
expands rubrics by 33–60% and Prune removes 8–20%, leaving rubrics 8–47%
larger than the generated baseline. In Round 2, Add expands rubrics by a
further 26–41% and Prune removes 4–15%, leaving final rubrics 19–82%
larger than the generated baseline. RubricBench sizes here are averaged
over all 1,147 tasks; Table
[7](#A3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ C.1 Rubric Sizes and Retained Human Preference Comparisons ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
reports 17.3 because it averages over the comparisons retained by the
$`\delta=0.10`$ margin.

We report rubric size as the mean number of criteria per task (rather
than raw totals) to enable comparison across benchmarks which differ
substantially in size. Table
[10](#A3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ C.3 Rubric Size and Category Composition ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
shows a consistent expand-then-contract pattern over the course of the
pipeline: in the first round, Add increases mean rubric size by
approximately 33-60%, and Prune removes 8-20% of the expanded criterion
set.

Critically, Prune does not revert the rubrics to their initial state:
after the first refinement round, the rubrics remain 8-47% larger than
the selected initial rubrics. The second refinement round follows the
same pattern, ending with rubrics that are 19-82% larger than the
initial rubrics.

Criteria are assigned to seven categories: Factual Accuracy, Safety,
Reasoning, Instruction Following, Style, Formatting, and Extraction.
Figure
[3](#A3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ C.3 Rubric Size and Category Composition ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
shows the different category distributions across benchmarks:
HealthBench allocates a larger share of criteria to Safety, while
Reasoning is particularly prominent in PRBench and ProfBench. The
category composition remains broadly similar across pipeline stages,
with a consistent shift toward Reasoning across all benchmarks.

### C.4 Model Inference Settings

##### Rubric generation and refinement.

GPT-5.1 used provider-default reasoning and temperature, while
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct used temperature $`0.7`$ and both had a
32,768-token output budget.

##### Generating assessment responses for each task.

The eight assessment models used a 32,768-token output budget (8,192 for
Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite), with provider-default reasoning for GPT-5.2
Instant and Gemini 3 Flash, high reasoning effort for GPT-5.2 Thinking
and Gemini 3.1 Pro, adaptive extended thinking for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and
Opus 4.6, and reasoning disabled for Gemini 2.5 Flash.

##### Verifying LLM responses against rubric criteria.

Our GPT-5 mini verifier used low reasoning effort, temperature $`1.0`$,
and a 512-token output budget.

### C.5 Post-training details

Table
[11](#A3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ C.5 Post-training details ‣ Appendix C Additional Results and Analysis ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")
summarizes the shared training configuration for RRD_(WU) and Rubricon.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Setting |  Value |
|  Base model |  Released Qwen3.5-9B post-trained checkpoint |
|  Training budget |  8 epochs; 152 updates |
|  Batch size |  Up to 64 prompts |
|  Responses per prompt |  8 sampled; at least 6 valid required |
|  Objective |  GRPO with no KL penalty or ratio clipping |
|  Optimizer |  Adam, constant learning rate $`10^{-5}`$ |
|  Adaptation |  LoRA rank 32 ([Hu et al., 2022](#bib.bib26)) |
|  Sampling |  Temperature 1.0 with maximum 4,096 generated tokens |
|  Reward |  Signed criterion score divided by total positive weight (Eq. [1](#S3.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 3 Task Formulation ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")) |
|  Advantages |  Rewards centered within each response group |
|  Failure handling |  Up to 3 grading attempts, discard groups with $`<`$ 6 valid responses |
|  Data order |  Same per-epoch shuffle across conditions, seed $`42+e`$ for epoch $`e`$ |

Table 11: Shared post-training configuration. This configuration was
identified to be effective by initially training on the original
(expert-authored) HealthBench rubrics, rather than tuning the
configuration based on training against automatically generated rubrics.

## Appendix D Limitations of Alternate Approaches in our Experiments

### D.1 Merging versus Refinement

We observe that pooling criteria from all $`K{=}5`$ candidate rubrics
produced in the Generate-and-Select stage provides broader coverage than
a single draft. To assess the benefits of pooling, we construct a merged
rubric containing all criteria from these drafts and compare it with
both the selected draft alone and the Rubricon rubric. The merged rubric
retains the criteria as generated, without deduplication or other
modification. We score the merged rubric by aggregating the
criterion-level verifier judgments already obtained for the five drafts,
so merging requires no additional generator or verifier calls.

Merging improves alignment with the human rubrics on all four
benchmarks, raising macro-average $`\rho`$ from $`0.364`$ for the
selected draft to $`0.402`$ for the merged rubric (Table
[12](#A4.T12 "Table 12 ‣ D.1 Merging versus Refinement ‣ Appendix D Limitations of Alternate Approaches in our Experiments ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
These gains come with a much larger rubric: the average rubric size
across benchmarks increases from $`20.6`$ to $`103.2`$ criteria per
task. Rubricon achieves a higher macro-average $`\rho`$ than the merged
rubric ($`0.428`$ vs $`0.402`$) with $`32.3`$ criteria per task,
$`3.2\times`$ fewer than if merged. These results suggest that broader
coverage alone is insufficient: Rubricon benefits from targeted addition
and pruning, rather than simply accumulating criteria.

|                 |           |       |          |      |          |       |             |      |
|-----------------|-----------|-------|----------|------|----------|-------|-------------|------|
|                 | ProfBench |       | ACE      |      | PRBench  |       | HealthBench |      |
| Rubric          | $`\rho`$  | Size  | $`\rho`$ | Size | $`\rho`$ | Size  | $`\rho`$    | Size |
| Selected rubric | 0.345     | 23.6  | 0.352    | 19.4 | 0.421    | 21.3  | 0.339       | 17.9 |
| Merged rubric   | 0.391     | 119.2 | 0.387    | 96.0 | 0.462    | 107.3 | 0.367       | 90.2 |
| Rubricon        | 0.424     | 41.9  | 0.385    | 25.0 | 0.516    | 38.8  | 0.388       | 23.4 |

Table 12: Alignment with expert-authored rubrics (Spearman $`\rho`$) and
average rubric size (criteria per task). Merging improves alignment over
the selected rubric at approximately $`5\times`$ the rubric size, while
Rubricon achieves higher macro-average alignment with a $`3.2\times`$
smaller rubric than the merge.

### D.2 Deduplication

Near-duplicate criteria can occasionally enter automatically-generated
rubrics, but are difficult to remove without discarding distinct but
related checks. We experimented with various LLM-based de-duplication
calls, and then aggregating the flagged criteria using either their
union or intersection. Taking the union was overly aggressive, flagging
distinct criteria as redundant, whereas taking the intersection left
duplicates unresolved. LLMs struggled to achieve an effective balance
between removing redundancy and preserving coverage. Although filtering
based on the more-conservative intersection could remove some
duplicates, the required LLM calls increased inference costs without
consistent gains in downstream rubric quality.

### D.3 Few-shot Rubric Examples

Following [Dhole and Agichtein (2026)](#bib.bib15), we experimented with
few-shot prompting by including expert-authored rubrics from other tasks
within the same dataset as examples of what a good rubric should look
like. We hypothesized that these examples would help communicate what a
rubric should cover and how detailed its criteria should be, but did not
observe an improvement in the resulting rubrics. This may be because
evaluation requirements differ significantly across tasks even within
the same dataset, limiting how applicable the few-shot examples are for
a new task. The extensive guidance already present in Rubricon initial
generation prompt may also reduce the additional value of few-shot
demonstrations.

### D.4 LLM-based Autograder to identify Flaws

We experimented with a refinement step in which a LLM autograder
compared a candidate response against an *expert reference response* (a
correct reference answer written by a human) to identify flaws in the
candidate response. Another LLM call then converted any flaws not
already covered by the existing rubric into additional criteria.
However, these additions tend to overfit to the expert response,
treating its particular details or solution choices as requirements.
Because a task may admit multiple correct answers, such criteria risk
penalizing valid alternatives simply for differing from a specific
expert response.

## Appendix E Rubricon Refinement Examples

Here we showcase how specific rubrics evolve over the stages of the
Rubricon pipeline. Each example presents a task and two model responses
(with their scores against an expert-authored rubric), followed by an
evolution of the Rubricon rubric through its Generate-and-Select, Add,
and Prune stages. We show the initial rubric, newly added criteria
(marked $`+`$), and removed criteria (struck through, with
automatically-generated removal reasons in parentheses).

Highlighted passages in the response connect response-wording to
specific criteria discussed in the accompanying analysis of each example
(Appendix
[E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Analysis of the Examples ‣ Appendix E Rubricon Refinement Examples ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training")).
Our analysis examines how iterative refinement of the rubric changes the
responses’ relative scores and compares their quality-ranking against
that according to the expert-authored rubric.

### E.1 Analysis of the Examples

##### Example 1: Iterative refinement expands coverage and restores expert alignment.

The strongest alignment with the human expert rubric is reached after
Prune. Across all eight assessment responses, $`\rho`$ rises from
$`0.420`$ to $`0.925`$, well above the initial rubric after the
Generate-and-Select stage ($`0.613`$). Add introduces four criteria,
including the need for urgent evaluation even if symptoms improve and
the importance of not delaying an ambulance in favor of driving to
hospital. Neither response explicitly addresses the first requirement,
showing how Add can help cover an omission shared by different
responses.

The physician-authored rubric scores Claude Sonnet 4.6’s response above
Gemini 2.5 Flash’s response ($`0.338`$ vs. $`0.208`$). The generated
rubric initially agrees, with a score margin of $`+0.042`$ in Claude
Sonnet 4.6’s favor, but Add reverses this ordering to $`-0.024`$. One
added criterion, "Does not state with absolute certainty that the
condition is or is not anaphylaxis or make guarantees about recovery or
outcome", penalizes categorical diagnostic claims. Claude Sonnet 4.6’s
response fails it by stating “what you’re describing is anaphylaxis,”
whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash’s response passes with “could be anaphylaxis.”
Prune removes this criterion along with other flagged criteria,
restoring the reference ordering with a margin of $`+0.056`$.

The criteria Prune removes score a dimension the reference rubric does
not and reward hedging over clarity. None of the physician-authored
criteria for this task addresses diagnostic certainty, and none of its
eight explicitly penalized failure modes concerns overconfident
phrasing. Three other removed criteria carry no discriminative signal in
our construction responses as they are satisfied by all model responses.
It is unlikely future responses would contain such flaws, and
exhaustively covering every conceivable failure mode is impractical.

Under the final rubric, three criteria distinguish the responses. Claude
Sonnet 4.6’s response receives credit for conditional positioning
instructions and preparing for CPR, while Gemini 2.5 Flash’s response
receives credit for advising against food or drink. The resulting
ordering agrees with the physician-authored rubric.

##### Example 2: Refinement keeps useful additions and removes misleading criteria.

The strongest alignment with the human expert rubric is reached after
Prune. Across the assessment responses for this task, $`\rho`$ falls
from $`0.632`$ at Generate-and-Select to $`0.531`$ after Add, then rises
to $`0.682`$ after Prune. Add introduces ten criteria covering practical
access and safety considerations, including criteria covering the
distinction between topical and injectable lidocaine, local healthcare
resources, and warning signs requiring urgent care.

The physician-authored rubric scores GPT-5.2 Thinking’s response
$`0.295`$ points above Gemini 3 Flash’s response. GPT-5.2’s response
explains when topical versus injectable lidocaine is needed, suggests
checks for counterfeit medicines, and asks what the user needs it for.
Gemini 3 Flash’s response omits these details and makes broader claims
about local availability. Criteria from the Add stage capture these
useful distinctions. For example, the added criterion "If the response
mentions lidocaine products that can be bought directly from a pharmacy
(such as gels, creams, or sprays), it clearly distinguishes these
over-the-counter topical forms for minor surface pain from injectable
lidocaine used for medical procedures and states that procedures like
suturing or tooth extraction still require a trained provider using
injectable anesthetic in a clinical setting" explicitly captures the
topical–injectable distinction.

Three criteria removed by Prune penalize GPT-5.2’s response relative to
Gemini 3 Flash’s response in ways that do not clearly reflect
substantive omissions. The consultation-disclaimer criterion, "Avoids
making definitive promises or diagnoses and, when giving advice, makes
it clear that the response does not replace an in-person consultation
with a qualified health professional", scores Gemini 3 Flash’s response
$`1`$ and GPT-5.2’s response $`0`$, rewarding explicit disclaimer
language despite GPT-5.2’s concrete guidance about seeking professional
care. The essential-medicine criterion, "If the response mentions
essential medicine status, it correctly states that lidocaine is
considered a basic or essential medicine (for example, on the WHO
Essential Medicines List or Nigeria’s essential medicines list)", scores
GPT-5.2’s response $`0`$ even though it does not mention
essential-medicine status, so the criterion’s stated condition is not
triggered. The brand-promotion criterion, "Does not promote specific
commercial brand names of lidocaine or other medications as superior or
required, focusing instead on the generic medicine and type of facility
needed", scores GPT-5.2’s response $`0.67`$, although it names Xylocaine
as an alternative name rather than promoting it. Together, these
criteria contribute an unnormalized weighted score difference of $`4.3`$
points in Gemini 3 Flash’s favor.

Prune retains seven of Add’s ten criteria, preserving expanded coverage
while removing criteria whose observed scoring behavior introduces
misleading distinctions between the responses.

## Appendix G Agent Rubric Generation Baseline

The Agentic baseline runs the GPT-5.1 model inside the Codex SDK agent
harness ([OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib24)) in a per-task Docker container.
Each task gets a fresh workspace directory mounted at /workspace; the
agent is started with sandbox=workspace_write and
approval_mode=auto_review, with the workspace as its working directory
and no extra developer instructions. Within this sandbox, the agent may
read and write files in the workspace and run shell and Python commands.
Network access for tool commands is disabled.

##### Workspace files.

The workspace contains prompt.txt, which is the rubric generation prompt
in Appendix
[F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Rubric Generation ‣ Appendix F Prompt Templates ‣ Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training"),
rendered with the task prompt only. No example responses or reference
material are included in the generation prompt. They are instead placed
in the workspace and surfaced to the agent via a provided AGENTS.md
file, shown below, which Codex loads as project-level instructions.
````
